artiklar.titel: Before particles: learning to see the world as quantum fields
artiklar.amne: Quantum field theory Fundamental interactions Particle physics Gauge theory Gravity

avsnitt.text: Imagine preparing a region so that no detector there registers a particle excitation. The intuitive picture says that nothing remains. Quantum field theory gives a stranger answer: the state can still possess vacuum correlations, and field variables remain part of the theory because particles are not its basic starting objects. Particles are particular, and sometimes only approximate, ways in which field states carry energy, momentum, spin, charge and other quantum numbers. [4] [5] This reversal is the conceptual doorway. Do not begin with four forces and ask which particle carries each one. Begin with fields, quantum states and couplings. The familiar catalogue of particles and forces then becomes a set of consequences. There is one more reversal to make. A quantum field is not quite a substance spread through space, like fog or water. That metaphor helps briefly, then fails. In common formulations a quantum field is represented by an operator valued distribution over spacetime. After smearing with test functions, it helps construct operators associated with finite spacetime regions. In algebraic formulations, algebras of observables are assigned directly to regions. These structures belong to a framework that predicts probabilities for possible measurement outcomes. Whether the field should also be regarded as literally what exists is an ontological interpretation, strongly motivated by the success and structure of the theory, but not separately photographed by an experiment. That distinction matters. Quantum field theory is experimentally extraordinary. A simple mental image of quantum fields is not itself an experimental result.

avsnitt.rubrik: Why fields enter the story at all
avsnitt.text: Quantum mechanics is often introduced as a theory of a fixed number of particles. One writes a wave function for one electron, then perhaps a more complicated wave function for two. That framework works beautifully when changes in particle number can be neglected. A fundamental local relativistic theory must, however, accommodate processes in which particle number changes. [1] [4] [5] Collision energy can produce massive particle excitations when the conservation laws and interaction dynamics allow it. Particles can also annihilate and transfer their energy into other excitations. A theory with a permanently fixed number of elementary objects is therefore too small for a fundamental local account of relativistic interactions. Quantum field theory solves this by changing the question. Instead of quantising the motion of a predetermined collection of particles, it quantises systems that can support zero, one, two or any allowed number of particle excitations. Creation and annihilation are then changes of state, not exceptions added after the fact. There is a second reason. Relativity demands a local account of influence. What happens in one region must not allow controllable information to jump instantaneously to a spacelike separated region. Quantum fields provide local observables while allowing quantum states to possess correlations across distance. This combination of local causal dynamics and nonclassical correlation is one of the deepest structural achievements of the theory. So fields are not introduced merely because physicists enjoy continuous mathematics. They provide a framework in which quantum theory, changing particle number and relativistic locality coexist.

avsnitt.rubrik: A scale map before the journey
avsnitt.text: The same physical world admits different useful descriptions at different scales. A planet is not best described as a state containing an enormous uncertain number of Standard Model quanta. A proton is not well described as three static coloured balls. A photon striking a detector is not well described only as a classical wave. The descriptions nest: quantum fields â†’ particles and bound states â†’ atoms â†’ materials â†’ classical objects . \text{quantum fields} \longrightarrow \text{particles and bound states} \longrightarrow \text{atoms} \longrightarrow \text{materials} \longrightarrow \text{classical objects}. Each arrow requires an approximation, a collective description or an effective theory. The more familiar level is not false. It suppresses details that cease to matter for the question being asked.

avsnitt.rubrik: First step: what physicists mean by a field
avsnitt.text: A classical field assigns something to every location and time. A temperature field assigns a number. The electromagnetic field assigns electric and magnetic vectors. The gravitational field in general relativity is encoded in spacetime geometry. A quantum field is not merely a classical field with small random wiggles. Quantum theory changes what counts as a physical state and what questions can have simultaneous definite answers. In operator formulations, fields enter as operator valued distributions acting on quantum states. The state determines probabilities for possible outcomes. Appropriately smeared, gauge invariant self adjoint combinations can represent local observables, while other field variables construct states and correlation functions without being separately measurable. This yields three ideas that should be kept separate: The field type tells us which kind of quantum degree of freedom the model contains, such as an electron field or electromagnetic field. The quantum state tells us the condition of all those fields, such as vacuum, one particle, many particles or an entangled state. A particle is a quantised excitation carrying characteristic quantum numbers, with energy and momentum either definite in an idealised mode or distributed across a wave packet. The concept is cleanest for free fields and for particles sufficiently far before or after an interaction. The last qualification is important. Inside a strongly interacting system, or in curved spacetime, the concept of a particle can become approximate or observer dependent. The field description is more general than the particle description.

avsnitt.rubrik: A field is not a wave function spread through space
avsnitt.text: The wave function of a single nonrelativistic particle and a quantum field are different kinds of object. A wave function describes the quantum state of that particle. A field operator is part of the theory's machinery for representing local physical quantities and changing field states. A state of the entire field can contain no particles, one particle, many particles or superpositions of different particle numbers. This distinction prevents a common confusion. The electron field does not become smaller because only one electron is present. The field type remains part of the theory. What changes is its quantum state. Nor should the phrase â€œat each pointâ€ be taken too literally. Quantum fields at mathematical points are singular objects. The rigorous quantities are normally smeared over finite regions with test functions, which is why physicists call them operator valued distributions. Real detectors also occupy finite regions and interact for finite times.

avsnitt.rubrik: From a chain to a continuous field
avsnitt.text: Imagine a long row of masses connected by springs. Each mass can move, but its motion affects its neighbours. A local push travels, disperses and reflects. The combined motion can also be decomposed into normal modes, each with its own frequency. Now reduce the spacing while increasing the number of masses. In a controlled limit the chain becomes a continuous classical field. This is a useful bridge because it reveals two complementary descriptions of the same dynamics. One description tracks what happens locally. The other tracks global modes. The continuum quantum theory is more subtle than an actual infinite spring chain. It requires careful treatment of arbitrarily short wavelengths, and the field at an exact point is not an ordinary observable. Still, the chain explains why local propagation and mode decomposition can coexist.

avsnitt.rubrik: A mental image that helps, if used carefully
avsnitt.text: The mathematics of field modes resembles an immense instrument with many possible resonances. A particle can resemble one quantum of excitation in a mode. This is a picture of the mode mathematics, not a proposal that space contains a vibrating material, and interacting fields need not preserve a simple one field, one particle correspondence.

Quantising a field does not imply that physical space is a lattice or that the field value can take only a list of discrete values. It means that the field has a quantum state, observables are represented by operators, alternatives can interfere, and energy transfer in suitable modes occurs in quanta. A field amplitude can even have a continuous range of possible measurement outcomes while its excitation energy is quantised. The discreteness belongs to particular observables and states, not automatically to spacetime itself.

avsnitt.rubrik: Second step: why quantum fields produce particles
avsnitt.text: A free bosonic field can be decomposed mathematically into modes. Each mode behaves like a quantum harmonic oscillator. A classical oscillator can have any energy. A quantum oscillator has discrete excitation levels. Moving from one level to the next changes the energy by a quantum. In a field, those quanta have the properties we associate with particles. [1] [4] [6] For one bosonic mode the energy levels take the form E n = â„ Ï‰ ( n + 1 2 ) . E_n=\hbar\omega\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right). The integer n n counts mode excitations. The zero point term does not mean that n = 0 n=0 contains half a detectable particle. It expresses the ground state energy of the oscillator representation. In nongravitational calculations only appropriately defined differences and renormalised quantities enter observations. Coupling vacuum energy consistently to gravity leads into the separate cosmological constant problem. Fermion fields, including electron and quark fields, are quantised differently. Their creation and annihilation operators anticommute, and a given single particle state cannot be occupied by two identical fermions. This is the field theoretic origin of Fermi statistics and the Pauli exclusion principle. Bosonic modes allow repeated occupation. Fermionic modes do not. For the electromagnetic field, a quantum is a photon. For the electron field, an excitation is an electron, while the corresponding antiparticle excitation is a positron. This is why quantum field theory naturally accommodates particle creation and annihilation. Energy can move between fields and change which particle excitations are present, while the theory preserves the relevant conservation laws. In the standard inertial flat spacetime description, the vacuum is the lowest energy state of the fields, not a classical void. It has quantum correlations and nonzero fluctuations of suitable observables. This does not mean that the vacuum is full of short lived ordinary particles constantly appearing in a directly observable way. That popular phrase confuses a calculational representation with a detector level event.

For a free field, states can be organised into a Fock space. Its sectors contain zero particles, one particle, two particles and so forth. Creation operators move a state upward by adding an excitation. Annihilation operators move it downward when an allowed excitation is present. [4] States may have a definite particle number or be superpositions of different number sectors. The construction is cleanest for free fields and asymptotic particle states. In a fully interacting theory, in thermal settings or in curved spacetime, the choice of particle modes and corresponding Fock representation can become more subtle. Gauge theories also contain redundant mathematical components, so not every formal excitation represents a physical state. This language can sound as if an operator were a miniature machine manufacturing objects. It is instead algebraic. It tells us how one state is related to another and how amplitudes are calculated. Still, it captures something physically decisive: particle number is a property of a state, not a fixed ingredient specified before the theory begins.

avsnitt.rubrik: Is a particle a local bump?
avsnitt.text: Not generally. A state of definite momentum is spread throughout space. A more localised wave packet requires a superposition of momenta. Interactions, detector resolution and relativistic constraints complicate localisation further. The most reliable operational meaning of a particle is often an energy and momentum quantum prepared or registered by an apparatus. This is why collider physicists infer particles from structured sets of tracks, energy deposits and missing momentum. A detector does not photograph a free standing field ripple. It records local interactions, and a theory connects the pattern of records to a particle hypothesis. Consider a one photon state spread across two possible detector locations. The state may be spatially delocalised, yet one ideal detector registers the full quantum of energy in a particular run. The extended state and the local event are not rival descriptions. They refer to different parts of the experimental account.

For free fields, and for well defined asymptotic particle states in Minkowski spacetime, inertial observers agree on the standard vacuum and positive frequency particle classification. In more general settings the split into positive and negative frequency modes can differ. Uniformly accelerated observers, for example, assign particle content differently from inertial observers in the Unruh analysis. This does not make detector records subjective. It shows that â€œparticleâ€ is not always a context free primitive, whereas the field framework survives. [9]

avsnitt.rubrik: Particles are clearest at the edges of an experiment
avsnitt.text: Scattering experiments have a natural grammar. Incoming states are prepared, an interaction occurs, and outgoing excitations are registered. Far before and after the interaction, the states can often be approximated as free particles. Inside the interacting region, a unique story about a fixed collection of individual particles may not exist. Quantum field theory connects the prepared and registered states through an amplitude. This is why particle language is experimentally precise without requiring every intermediate stage to be a hidden particle trajectory.

avsnitt.rubrik: Third step: locality without classical separability
avsnitt.text: We can now state more precisely what was only promised at the beginning: quantum field theory combines local observable dynamics with globally nonseparable quantum states. [5] Relativistic quantum field theory combines two statements that initially seem incompatible. First, operations in spacelike separated regions cannot be used to send information faster than light. In formal language, suitable gauge invariant local observables commute at spacelike separation. This condition is called microcausality. Second, the quantum state can contain correlations between those regions that no classical local model can reproduce. Entanglement does not carry a controllable message by itself, so it does not violate relativistic causality. A useful mental distinction is between dynamics and state . The dynamics is local. The state need not factorise into independent pieces for every region. The theory can therefore satisfy microcausality and prohibit faster than light signalling without making the world a collection of locally self contained classical parts. This matters for understanding fields. A field is not merely a value stored independently at each point. The physically relevant object includes patterns of correlation between possible local measurements.

avsnitt.rubrik: Fourth step: a force becomes a coupling
avsnitt.text: In classical mechanics, a force changes the motion of an object. In quantum field theory the deeper description is an interaction term, or coupling, in the theory. It specifies how states of one or more fields can influence one another and which transformations are allowed. Much of that information is compressed into an action, S = âˆ« d 4 x â„’ . S=\int d^4x\,\mathcal{L}. The Lagrangian density â„’ \mathcal{L} identifies the fields, their free propagation and their permitted couplings. This expression is not a visual explanation, but it is the formal centre of the subject. To understand a quantum field theory is, in large part, to understand which terms may occur in â„’ \mathcal{L} , which symmetries constrain them and how their predictions depend on energy scale. For example, the electron field couples to the electromagnetic field because the electron carries electric charge. That coupling permits processes in which an electron emits or absorbs a photon. It also produces the electromagnetic interaction between charged systems. The simplest schematic example is a product of fields in the Lagrangian. In quantum electrodynamics the interaction has the form â„’ i n t = âˆ’ e Ïˆ â€¾ Î³ Î¼ A Î¼ Ïˆ . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}=-e\,\bar{\psi}\gamma^\mu A_\mu\psi. Here Ïˆ \psi represents the electron and positron field, A Î¼ A_\mu the electromagnetic gauge field and e e the coupling. The expression is not a picture of one object touching another. It is a local rule for how the combined quantum state can evolve.

Quantum field theory usually predicts amplitudes. An amplitude is not an ordinary probability. Alternatives must first be combined as complex amplitudes, allowing interference, and only then converted into probabilities. Experiments repeat a preparation many times and compare the resulting distribution of events with quantities such as cross sections and decay rates. This is the bridge between the smooth mathematical field language and the discrete marks in a detector. The field theory predicts a probability distribution. Each run produces a particular macroscopic record.

A two point function encodes a relation between field insertions at two spacetime locations. Its interpretation depends on the object used. A retarded Green function describes causal response and, in a local relativistic theory, has support only in or on the future light cone of the source. A Feynman propagator is a time ordered correlation used in perturbative amplitudes. In a Feynman diagram an internal line represents such a propagator. Calling that line a travelling virtual particle adds a story that the mathematics does not require. [3] The distinction is clearest when several diagrams contribute. No single diagram is an observable history. The measurable prediction follows from the sum of all required contributions at the chosen approximation order, with gauge dependent contributions cancelling in consistently calculated physical observables at that order. A Feynman propagator need not vanish at spacelike separation. This does not enable faster than light signalling, because the signal carrying response and the commutators of physical local observables retain the required causal structure.

avsnitt.rubrik: A path integral is not a film either
avsnitt.text: Another formulation assigns an amplitude by summing over field configurations, weighted by their action. This is the path integral. The phrase â€œthe particle takes every pathâ€ is an evocative mnemonic, not a literal account of many hidden classical journeys. The integration is a procedure for constructing a quantum amplitude. Which histories count as intermediate terms depends on the chosen variables and formulation, while the observable predictions do not. [2] So the sentence â€œforces happen because particles are exchangedâ€ is useful only after repair: Interacting quantum fields produce amplitudes that can sometimes be organised mathematically as exchanges of field quanta. The observable content lies in the complete amplitude and its predicted probabilities, not in an invisible microscopic story attached to each internal line.

The electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions are gauge field theories. This phrase is often explained too quickly. [10] [28] A gauge description contains representational freedom. Different mathematical field configurations can describe the same physical situation. Requiring the description to remain consistent when that representation is chosen independently at different points in spacetime introduces a geometric structure called a connection. In particle physics, the associated connection is represented by gauge fields. Suppose the complex phase convention for an electron field may be chosen differently at neighbouring locations. An ordinary derivative would then confuse a change of convention with a physical change. The gauge connection supplies the correction needed to compare the field consistently from place to place. In QED this appears through the covariant derivative D Î¼ = âˆ‚ Î¼ + i e A Î¼ , D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ieA_\mu, where A Î¼ A_\mu is the electromagnetic gauge potential. The combined expression transforms consistently even when the local phase convention changes.

Imagine that every location carries its own convention for what direction counts as zero on an internal compass. Comparing two arrows at different locations then requires a rule for transporting the convention between them. The connection supplies that rule. Curvature records whether transport around a loop returns the convention unchanged. This analogy captures the geometric logic but must not be made literal. The internal spaces of the Standard Model are not ordinary directions in physical space. Gauge transformations change the descriptive convention, not the underlying physical situation. Gauge invariant quantities, including field strengths and observable amplitudes, carry the empirical content. It is tempting to say that local gauge symmetry â€œcausesâ€ forces. That statement is too strong without qualification. Gauge symmetry is a redundancy of description, and merely writing a redundancy cannot create physics. Yet the requirement of local gauge consistency, combined with locality, relativistic quantum theory, the chosen matter content and dynamics, severely constrains the possible interaction terms. This structure organises the electromagnetic, weak and strong theories with remarkable success. The gauge groups of the Standard Model are written S U ( 3 ) C Ã— S U ( 2 ) L Ã— U ( 1 ) Y . SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y. The symbols are not labels pasted onto three forces. They encode allowed transformations and the charges to which the corresponding gauge fields respond. Matter fields occupy representations of these groups. A charge tells us how a field transforms. Electric charge, weak isospin, hypercharge and colour charge are therefore not tiny substances stored inside a particle. They specify how the corresponding field participates in the symmetry and interaction structure.

The order of two U ( 1 ) U(1) transformations does not matter. This makes electromagnetism an Abelian gauge theory. In S U ( 2 ) SU(2) and S U ( 3 ) SU(3) , transformations need not commute. Their gauge fields can consequently carry the relevant gauge charge and couple to one another. This self interaction is especially visible in QCD and is central to why gluon dynamics differs so much from photon dynamics.

avsnitt.rubrik: A microscope changes the apparent interaction
avsnitt.text: Imagine measuring electric charge at different resolutions. The quantum vacuum responds to a charged source, and the effective interaction depends on how closely it is probed. In QED the electromagnetic coupling grows slowly toward higher energies. In QCD the gluon contribution reverses the overall trend, making the strong coupling smaller at high energies. [11] [25] Running is not a flaw or an illusion. The scale dependence of consistently defined effective charges and its consequences for observables are measurable predictions, although the numerical renormalised coupling depends on the chosen definition and scheme. What counts as the effective charge depends on the scale at which surrounding quantum effects have been resolved. Renormalisation is the rule for translating between descriptions made at different resolutions while preserving the same observable physics. A coupling is not generally one fixed number at every resolution. Quantum fluctuations make the effective coupling depend on the energy or distance scale at which it is measured. In the Wilsonian picture, short wavelength degrees of freedom are successively removed from an explicit description. Their effects remain encoded in changed couplings and additional allowed terms. Different microscopic systems can consequently flow toward the same large scale behaviour. Regularisation and renormalisation should not be confused. A regulator controls otherwise ill defined short distance contributions, for example through a momentum cutoff or dimensional continuation. In a continuum calculation it is removed after parameters and operators have been renormalised. In an effective theory a cutoff may instead mark the theory's domain. Renormalisation connects the theory's parameters to quantities fixed by measurement at a stated scale. Consistently calculated observables are regulator independent up to truncation errors and higher order terms. The modern effective field theory viewpoint adds a powerful principle. A theory can make precise low energy predictions even if it is not the final theory at arbitrarily high energy. Additional interaction terms are organised by how strongly they are suppressed by a higher energy scale. This is why saying that a theory is not perturbatively renormalisable does not mean that it is useless. Gravity is the crucial example.

avsnitt.rubrik: Effective does not mean approximate in a careless sense
avsnitt.text: An effective field theory includes the most general local interactions among its chosen low energy degrees of freedom that are compatible with the symmetries, organised by a stated power counting and the scale suppressing higher order terms. At low enough energy only a finite number matter to a requested precision. The framework can therefore make systematically improvable predictions while remaining deliberately silent about unknown shorter distance physics. This is a general scientific lesson. A theory need not answer every possible scale to be exact enough within a stated domain.

avsnitt.rubrik: How a quantum field becomes a classical field
avsnitt.text: Before applying this framework to the four interactions, we need one final bridge: how the quantum description recovers the classical fields and forces with which the interaction stories usually begin. [7] [8] If the world is quantum fields, why does a radio wave look like a smooth classical electromagnetic field rather than a rain of conspicuous photons? One part of the answer is occupation number. A classical electromagnetic wave can correspond approximately to a coherent quantum state involving an indefinite but typically large number of photons. For free or effectively linear dynamics, and approximately over suitable timescales in weakly interacting settings, relevant field expectation values can follow classical equations while relative quantum fluctuations remain small. Large occupation number alone is not sufficient. A many photon number state can remain strongly nonclassical. Environmental decoherence and coarse graining can suppress observable interference between selected alternatives and stabilise an effective classical description of the variables being tracked. This explains much of the quantum to classical transition, but decoherence alone does not by itself select one unique measurement outcome. So the relation is not â€œquantum particles underneath, classical fields on topâ€. Both particle like and classical field like behaviour are possible regimes of quantum fields.

avsnitt.rubrik: The classical force as a limit
avsnitt.text: Coulomb's law can be recovered from QED in an appropriate low energy, nonrelativistic limit. A classical electromagnetic field can also arise as an expectation value in suitable quantum states. These are two compatible reductions of the same theory. The everyday word force is therefore not discarded. It is recovered. Quantum field theory explains the conditions under which a simpler force law becomes reliable. We can now examine each interaction at three levels: its quantum field structure, its observable excitations and its classical or effective limit.

Quantum electrodynamics describes the coupling of electrically charged fields to the electromagnetic gauge field. Its gauge structure is associated with U ( 1 ) U(1) . The observable quantum of the electromagnetic field is the photon. [28] The photon is massless. In the field equations this permits electromagnetic effects with unlimited range, although actual fields can be screened or cancelled by surrounding charges. Photons do not carry electric charge, so the electromagnetic field does not have the same direct self interaction structure as the gluon field. At low energy, two slowly moving charges feel a potential proportional to V ( r ) âˆ q 1 q 2 r . V(r)\propto \frac{q_1q_2}{r}. This familiar expression is not inserted independently into QED. It emerges from the quantum field interaction in the appropriate static limit. The sign of the product of the charges distinguishes attraction from repulsion. Masslessness helps explain the unlimited range, but it is not by itself sufficient to guarantee an observable long range force. Gluons are also massless in the Standard Model, yet confinement prevents a simple long range colour force between isolated objects. Range depends on the complete dynamics and on which physical states can exist. Photons have no direct elementary self coupling in the QED Lagrangian because U ( 1 ) U(1) is Abelian. Photon scattering can nevertheless occur through quantum loops of charged fields. â€œPhotons do not interactâ€ is therefore only a lowest order shorthand. The everyday solidity of a table is largely electromagnetic in origin, together with the Pauli exclusion principle for electrons. It is not primarily the strong nuclear force acting between the table and your hand.

avsnitt.rubrik: What the photon does and does not prove
avsnitt.text: Individual photons are established detector level excitations. The electromagnetic field is established through the enormous predictive coherence of classical electrodynamics and QED. But observing a photon does not reveal a tiny piece of field substance. It reveals an event whose energy, momentum, polarisation and statistics match the field theory.

The weak interaction acts on quarks and leptons and can change particle identity. It is central to beta decay, neutrino interactions and the reaction chains that power stars. In the Standard Model it is not an independent gauge theory placed beside electromagnetism. Both arise within the electroweak structure S U ( 2 ) L Ã— U ( 1 ) Y SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y . [12] [13] [28] In the usual gauge fixed description, the Higgs field has a nonzero vacuum expectation value. The gauge invariant physical content is that the theory lies in a Higgs phase whose spectrum contains massive W + W^+ , W âˆ’ W^- and Z 0 Z^0 bosons, a massless photon and a scalar Higgs excitation. The electroweak Lagrangian contains three S U ( 2 ) L SU(2)_L gauge fields, W 1 W^1 , W 2 W^2 and W 3 W^3 , and one hypercharge field, B B . The charged combinations are W Â± = W 1 âˆ“ i W 2 2 . W^{\pm}=\frac{W^1\mp iW^2}{\sqrt{2}}. The neutral mass eigenstates are mixtures, A = B cos Î¸ W + W 3 sin Î¸ W , A=B\cos\theta_W+W^3\sin\theta_W, Z = âˆ’ B sin Î¸ W + W 3 cos Î¸ W . Z=-B\sin\theta_W+W^3\cos\theta_W. The weak mixing angle Î¸ W \theta_W determines the combination and, as a renormalised quantity, depends on scale and convention. This is a concrete meaning of electroweak unification: electromagnetic and weak phenomena are different low energy manifestations of one shared gauge and coupling structure, not two substances that literally merge at a threshold. For a simple massive field, the static Green function produces a Yukawa type suppression beyond a characteristic length. This helps explain why low energy weak effects are short ranged without requiring a picture of particles flying between objects. A schematic static potential contains a factor like V ( r ) âˆ e âˆ’ m c r / â„ r . V(r)\propto \frac{e^{-mcr/\hbar}}{r}. The associated length scale is roughly â„ / ( m c ) \hbar/(mc) . The large masses of the W W and Z Z therefore make weak processes strongly suppressed at distances much larger than about 10 âˆ’ 18 10^{-18} metres. This formula is a guide to range, not a complete description of the chiral electroweak theory. The weak interaction also differs from electromagnetism in a conceptually radical way. It is chiral. The charged weak interaction couples to left handed fermion fields and right handed antifermion fields. Nature distinguishes handedness in weak processes, which is why mirror reflection is not a symmetry of the full Standard Model dynamics. Through quark mixing, a charged weak interaction can change one quark flavour into another. Through lepton mixing and nonzero neutrino mass differences, neutrino flavour states oscillate during propagation. These phenomena show why â€œforceâ€ is an incomplete word. A weak interaction can transform identity rather than merely push an object. [26] The Higgs field also allows charged leptons and quarks to acquire masses through Yukawa couplings. It is misleading, however, to say simply that â€œthe Higgs gives everything massâ€. The minimal Standard Model predicts massless neutrinos and must be extended to accommodate the observed masses. Whether the underlying mechanism is Dirac, Majorana or something more elaborate remains unknown. Most of the mass of protons and neutrons, and therefore most of the mass of ordinary matter, arises from quantum chromodynamic energy rather than directly from the Higgs contribution to the light quark masses.

The standard phrase electroweak symmetry breaking is useful but potentially misleading. A local gauge transformation is a redundancy of description, and a redundancy does not literally break like the rotational symmetry of a physical object. In a gauge fixed formulation the Higgs vacuum is described using spontaneous symmetry breaking. The gauge invariant physical statement is that the Higgs phase reorganises the spectrum and couplings: W W and Z Z are massive, the photon remains massless, and a scalar Higgs excitation appears. [14] [15]

For a free massive excitation the relation is [21] [22] E 2 = p 2 c 2 + m 2 c 4 . E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4. Mass here characterises how energy depends on momentum. It is not microscopic drag. The Higgs vacuum changes the allowed excitation spectrum without slowing particles through friction. The Higgs boson is a quantum excitation around the Higgs field's vacuum state. Its discovery, followed by measurements of its spin, parity and couplings, provided crucial evidence that the observed scalar is the Higgs boson of the electroweak mechanism. The boson is not continuously exchanged to maintain the mass of every object. [21] [22]

Quantum chromodynamics, QCD, describes quark and gluon fields. Its gauge structure is S U ( 3 ) C SU(3)_C , where C C refers to colour charge. Colour is a quantum property, not visual colour. [16] [17] [18] [28] QCD contains eight gauge field components forming the adjoint representation of S U ( 3 ) C SU(3)_C . In short distance perturbative calculations their quanta are called gluons. Unlike the photon, the nonabelian gauge fields carry colour charge and have direct self couplings in the QCD Lagrangian. Colour and anticolour labels are useful basis dependent bookkeeping, but isolated gluons are not gauge invariant asymptotic states in confining QCD. At very high momentum transfer, or equivalently very short distances, the effective strong coupling becomes weaker. This is asymptotic freedom. In the vacuum at hadronic scales the coupling becomes strong, perturbative calculations fail, and isolated coloured asymptotic states are not observed. Instead, the physical spectrum contains colour neutral hadrons. This confinement pattern is strongly supported by experiment and lattice QCD, but a complete analytic derivation for realistic four dimensional QCD with dynamical quarks remains unavailable. The rigorous Yang Mills existence and mass gap problem concerns pure Yang Mills theory and is related to, but not identical with, QCD confinement. Deep inelastic scattering revealed point like partonic constituents inside protons. At high momentum transfer, asymptotic freedom makes quark and gluon descriptions calculable. Yet detectors receive hadronic jets, not isolated quarks or gluons. For separated heavy colour sources, lattice calculations support a narrow flux tube whose energy initially grows with separation. With dynamical quarks the tube can break through quark and antiquark pair production, yielding new colour neutral hadrons. The flux tube is therefore a useful regime, not a universal literal string. This transition from useful quark and gluon degrees of freedom at short distance to hadrons at long distance is called hadronisation. It is an excellent warning against treating a particle catalogue as independent of scale. The dominant interaction binding protons and neutrons in nuclei is a residual low energy consequence of QCD, somewhat as intermolecular forces are residual consequences of electromagnetism. It is not identical to the fundamental colour interaction inside hadrons. At nuclear scales, chiral effective field theory uses nucleons, pions and contact interactions as the relevant degrees of freedom. One pion exchange gives the longest range leading contribution, while two pion exchange, shorter range contact terms and three nucleon forces enter systematically at higher orders. Pions are composite hadrons in this effective description, not elementary force carriers of a separate fundamental interaction. [20]

The light quarks' Higgs generated current masses account directly for only a small fraction of a proton's mass. The proton mass is the total rest energy of a strongly coupled QCD bound state and remains largely nonzero even in the light quark chiral limit. Statements that divide it into quark motion, gluon energy, interaction terms and trace contributions depend on the chosen renormalisation scheme and scale, although the total mass does not. Lattice QCD calculates the light hadron spectrum from the underlying theory with high precision. [19] It is therefore simultaneously true that the Higgs field is essential for the masses of elementary quarks and that most of the mass in a human body is associated with QCD dynamics inside nucleons. These statements refer to different levels in the causal chain.

avsnitt.rubrik: Gravity, the fourth interaction and the honest exception
avsnitt.text: The Standard Model is a quantum field theory of three fundamental interactions. Gravity is not its fourth gauge sector. [23] [24] [27] In general relativity, gravity is described by the dynamical geometry of spacetime. Its source is stress energy, which includes energy, momentum, pressure and stress, not merely rest mass. The geometry in turn influences motion. This classical theory has passed demanding tests, including the observation of gravitational waves. Calling gravity a force is often convenient, but freely falling objects in general relativity follow the straightest available paths, geodesics, in curved spacetime. An astronaut in orbit feels weightless not because gravity has vanished, but because both astronaut and spacecraft follow nearby free fall trajectories. What is locally measurable as gravitational stretching or squeezing is connected to spacetime curvature. At energies far below the Planck scale, general relativity supplies the leading term of a gravitational effective field theory. Perturbations of the metric about a suitable background can be quantised, and the corresponding massless spin two quanta are called gravitons. The framework yields systematically controlled low energy quantum corrections, although no specifically quantum gravitational correction has yet been isolated experimentally. The graviton is therefore a theoretical excitation of the perturbative effective theory, not an observed particle. Consistent coupling of a massless spin two field, under standard assumptions, leads to the universal coupling to stress energy characteristic of gravity. Classical gravitational wave detection is not graviton detection. Pure Einstein gravity is not perturbatively renormalisable as a fundamental theory with only finitely many parameters. At increasing order, higher curvature operators are required, with coefficients not fixed by low energy general relativity. Far below the cutoff they are suppressed and predictivity is retained order by order. Near the Planck regime the expansion ceases to be sufficient, and no experimentally established ultraviolet completion is known. [24] The conflict is therefore subtler than the slogan â€œquantum mechanics and relativity are incompatibleâ€. Quantum mechanics, special relativity and fields are successfully combined in the Standard Model. Quantum effects of gravity can be organised reliably at low energy. What is missing is an experimentally established account valid when quantum spacetime fluctuations can no longer be treated as small corrections. Candidate frameworks include string theory, loop based approaches, asymptotic safety and other programmes. None has received decisive experimental confirmation. Listing them is a map of research, not a list of established alternatives from which one can presently choose a winner. Therefore two common claims both need correction: â€œGravity has not been quantised in any senseâ€ is too strong. A perturbative low energy quantisation exists and is predictive within its domain, but gravity's quantum character has not been directly established experimentally. â€œThe graviton puts gravity on the same established footing as the photonâ€ is also false. No graviton has been detected, and the ultraviolet completion is unknown.

avsnitt.rubrik: Why â€œfour forcesâ€ is useful but not final
avsnitt.text: The phrase four fundamental interactions is a useful phenomenological classification: electromagnetic, weak, strong and gravitational. It is not the deepest organisational map. Electromagnetism and weak phenomena arise from one electroweak gauge structure. At nuclear energies the fundamental colour interaction is usually encountered indirectly through hadrons and residual nuclear forces. Gravity belongs to neither gauge sector of the Standard Model. Physicists investigate whether the strong interaction joins the electroweak structure at still higher energies, and whether gravity can be incorporated in a deeper framework. Grand unification remains hypothetical. The measured running couplings provide clues, but the Standard Model alone does not make all three gauge couplings meet at one experimentally confirmed unification point. There is also no universal, context free ranking of force â€œstrengthâ€. Couplings run with energy, gravity couples to stress energy, confinement changes what can be isolated, and macroscopic outcomes depend on charge cancellation and accumulation. Gravity dominates astronomy not because its microscopic coupling is large, but because ordinary bulk matter sources gravity with the same overall sign and there is no observed gravitational analogue of electrical charge screening, while macroscopic matter is usually nearly electrically neutral.

avsnitt.rubrik: Not every boson is a force carrier
avsnitt.text: The Standard Model contains bosonic fields, but â€œbosonâ€ and â€œforce carrierâ€ are not synonyms. The Higgs boson has spin zero and is not a gauge boson. Composite particles can also be bosons. Conversely, the useful description of an interaction need not be a picture of one boson travelling between two objects. [6] Spin classifies how a quantum state transforms under rotations and Lorentz transformations. The spin statistics theorem links physical integer spin excitations with Bose statistics and half integer spin excitations with Fermi statistics under assumptions including Lorentz covariance, locality, a stable vacuum and positive norm. It explains contrasting many particle behaviour of bosons and fermions, not a universal division between matter fields and gauge fields.

Return to a stone held in your hand. At one scale it is a single object with a surface, shape and weight. At a deeper scale it is a stable many body state involving electron fields, electromagnetic fields and atomic nuclei. The nuclei contain protons and neutrons, which are themselves strongly coupled states of quark and gluon fields. Most of the stone's rest mass comes from QCD dynamics within its nucleons. Its chemical identity and rigidity depend primarily on electromagnetic interactions and the quantum structure of electrons. The Pauli exclusion principle helps organise electrons into distinct states, but it is not an additional force. Gravity gives the stone weight near Earth, although its gravitational interaction is negligible in determining the internal structure of each atom. No single level cancels the others. â€œStoneâ€, â€œcrystal latticeâ€, â€œatomâ€, â€œnucleonâ€ and â€œquantum field stateâ€ are descriptions with different resolutions and explanatory tasks. Reduction does not mean that only the lowest level is scientifically real or useful. This is perhaps the most important systems lesson in the article. Fundamental laws constrain higher levels, but collective organisation creates new stable variables and effective rules. Understanding the world requires both the downward question, â€œWhat is this made from?â€, and the upward question, â€œWhich patterns become autonomous at this scale?â€

avsnitt.rubrik: A learning route that can be tested
avsnitt.text: Do not try to memorise the Standard Model diagram first. Work through the conceptual dependencies in order. Each stage has a question that reveals whether the idea is stable enough to support the next one. Stage Idea to master Checkpoint 1 Classical fields and local dynamics Can a field carry energy through a region containing no matter? 2 Modes and the quantum oscillator Why does quantised mode energy not imply pixelated space? 3 Field, state and particle What changes when one electron is added: the field type or its state? 4 Locality and correlation How can spacelike regions be entangled without enabling faster than light signalling? 5 Couplings and amplitudes Why is an interaction term more fundamental than a classical force arrow? 6 Gauge structure Which parts of a gauge description are convention, and which combinations are observable? 7 Renormalisation and scale Why can the measured effective coupling change when resolution changes? 8 The four interaction stories Why can electromagnetism, QCD and gravity not all be understood through the same messenger metaphor? 9 Classical and effective limits How can a smooth radio wave and a discrete photon detection arise from the same quantum field? If any checkpoint remains vague, returning one stage is more productive than adding another particle name. The difficulty in QFT is rarely the catalogue. It is keeping distinct concepts from collapsing into one another.

Experiments directly record tracks, energy deposits, timing signals, spectra and other macroscopic detector outcomes. Their distributions include neutral weak current events, resonant signatures and decay patterns attributed to W W , Z Z and Higgs bosons, and hadronic jets whose properties match quark and gluon initiated QCD calculations. Scale dependent cross sections support the predicted running of couplings. Together these observations provide exceptionally strong, but theory mediated, evidence for the Standard Model's quantum field structure. Orbital tests, clock comparisons, light propagation and gravitational wave signals strongly support classical general relativity and a dynamical spacetime metric. They do not yet establish gravitons or any specifically quantum property of gravity. [21] [22] [27] [28]

Fields, quantum states, gauge redundancies, Lagrangians, renormalisation and Feynman amplitudes form the mathematical machinery connecting experimental preparations to probability distributions for outcomes. The agreement of predictions derived from this machinery with experiment is empirical evidence for the framework. It does not by itself select one unique ontology or everyday visualisation of fields.

Whether fields alone constitute fundamental reality is a philosophical interpretation constrained by physics, not a separately measured fact. A complete quantum theory of gravity is unknown. Dark matter, dark energy, the origin of Standard Model parameters, the matter antimatter asymmetry and possible unification beyond the electroweak interaction also remain open.

The field perspective clarifies the known theory, but it also makes the boundaries of knowledge sharper. What fixes the Standard Model's gauge group, particle representations and three generations? What determines the Yukawa couplings and therefore the wide pattern of elementary fermion masses? What mechanism gives neutrinos mass, and are neutrinos Dirac or Majorana particles? Why is the strong CP parameter extraordinarily small? Can confinement in realistic QCD with dynamical quarks be derived with greater analytic control? Can a nontrivial pure Yang Mills quantum theory in four dimensions be constructed rigorously and proved to possess a mass gap? Do the gauge interactions unify in a larger structure at higher energy? What is the ultraviolet quantum theory of gravity, and can gravity's quantum character be demonstrated experimentally? Which field or other degree of freedom accounts for dark matter? What dynamics generated the observed cosmic matter antimatter asymmetry, given that Standard Model CP violation appears insufficient? Why does the observed cosmological constant differ so dramatically from naive quantum field estimates of vacuum energy? These are not loose ends around an otherwise final theory. They identify where the present framework stops speaking with established authority.

The Standard Model represents elementary matter and three nongravitational interactions using quantum fields. In regimes where particle states are well defined, particles are quantised field excitations. The interactions are structured couplings constrained by gauge symmetry, not necessarily exchanges of little messengers. The Higgs phase reorganises the electroweak spectrum and its Yukawa couplings generate the observed charged fermion mass parameters. Most ordinary rest mass, however, comes from QCD bound state dynamics. General relativity represents gravity as dynamical spacetime geometry and can serve as the leading term of a low energy quantum effective theory, but neither gravitons nor a high energy completion have been established experimentally. Once this is understood, the four forces stop looking like four invisible hands. They become four patterns in how physical degrees of freedom can exist, couple and change.

If an electron is an excitation of the electron field, what remains when no electron is present? Why is a virtual photon not simply a real photon that we fail to detect? What does photon mass have to do with the range of electromagnetism? Why do gluons make the strong interaction qualitatively different from electromagnetism? Which part of the mass of an ordinary stone is most directly connected to the Higgs field, and which part is mainly QCD energy? In what precise sense is gravity already a quantum field theory, and in what sense is quantum gravity unresolved?
