avsnitt.text: The Disengaged Teen , published in 2025 by journalist Jenny Anderson and Brookings scholar Rebecca Winthrop, argues that adults routinely misread how young people relate to school. We notice attendance, compliance, resistance, and grades. We are less good at seeing whether a student is curious, emotionally connected, thinking deeply, or acting with a sense of authorship. The book combines established engagement research, interviews, family stories, and a large Brookings and Transcend survey to describe four modes: Passenger, Achiever, Resister, and Explorer. [1] [2] [4] The labels are deliberately states rather than traits. A student can be an Explorer in theatre, a Passenger in mathematics, an Achiever during examination season, and a Resister when a task feels pointless or humiliating. The goal is not to type the child. It is to help the child notice the current mode, understand what produced it, and move intentionally when another mode would serve learning better. This qualification is essential. Remove it, and a flexible conversation tool becomes another set of boxes adults can use against adolescents. [2] [3] The book's central distinction is well aligned with research. School engagement has long been studied as behavioral, emotional, and cognitive, not merely as attendance or effort. Later research added agentic engagement: the student's constructive contribution to the conditions of learning. [8] [9] Self-determination research likewise finds that autonomy, competence, and relatedness help explain why motivation becomes more internalized and durable. [12] [13] But evidence congruence is not the same as validation. The four named modes are a synthesis of related constructs, not a clinically or psychometrically established taxonomy. The survey is large, but size cannot by itself prove that its cut points reveal four natural categories, that one mode causes a mental health outcome, or that an intervention moving a teenager from one quadrant to another will produce the outcomes associated with that quadrant. The Brookings report describes separate student and parent surveys, not a documented national sample of matched parent-child pairs. Its famous perception gaps are therefore best read as differences between populations, not proof that a specific parent misreads a specific child. [4] Strongest idea Compliance and achievement can conceal shallow, anxious, or externally controlled learning. Best-supported practice Support autonomy and relevance while preserving explicit teaching, competence building, and clear structure. Largest overreach Treating survey profiles as if they establish four validated kinds or a simple causal route from disengagement to distress. Best use A temporary language for better questions, never a verdict about who a teenager is. The most useful question in the book is not â€œWhich type is my child?â€ It is â€œWhat relationship to learning is this situation inviting?â€

The book begins from a failure of adult perception. Schools are built to make certain behaviors visible: arriving, sitting, submitting, passing, disrupting. Inner relations to learning are harder to see. A quiet student who completes the minimum may be coded as fine. A high-performing student who is terrified of error may be celebrated. A student who objects to an incoherent task may be defined by the objection. A student pursuing a difficult question for reasons of their own can look inefficient. This is why the book's most unsettling character is not the obvious rebel but the good student. The Passenger has learned how little genuine attention a system may require. The Achiever has learned how thoroughly external success can organize a life. Both can move through school without the visible crisis that triggers adult concern. The Resister, by contrast, makes the conflict legible. The Explorer does something still more demanding: participates in constructing the learning rather than merely receiving or defeating it. The distinction does not imply that every lesson should feel thrilling. Serious learning includes repetition, memory, frustration, and work whose value emerges late. Research on motivation suggests that personally valuing a task can sustain persistence even when the task is not intrinsically enjoyable. [13] The book is strongest when Explorer means agentic and meaningfully engaged, not permanently entertained. It is weaker whenever exploration sounds like a mood adults can manufacture by making every exercise fun. Mental image: four desks, one student At the first desk, the student waits for the bell. At the second, she calculates what earns the highest mark. At the third, she pushes the paper away. At the fourth, she asks whether the method could work on a different problem. These need not be four children. They may be four hours in one child's day.

Anderson and Winthrop make five linked claims. First, the language of engagement should describe not only observable effort but emotion, thought, and agency. Second, adolescents have a developmental need to test possibilities and exercise increasing authorship, while many schools narrow choice and relevance just as that need grows. Third, adults mistake visible compliance and performance for a healthy relationship to learning. Fourth, parents can help without becoming teachers by changing the questions, emotional climate, and distribution of control around schoolwork. Fifth, education should move from an â€œage of achievementâ€ toward an â€œage of agency,â€ preparing young people to direct learning across an unpredictable life. [2] [5] The argument has moral as well as empirical force. It says that education is not complete when a young person can satisfy instructions. A democratic and rapidly changing society needs people who can identify a problem, seek help, revise a strategy, tolerate uncertainty, and act in concert with others. A school can produce impressive scores while weakening some of those capacities if students experience learning chiefly as the management of adult demands. Yet the opposition between achievement and agency can be overstated. Knowledge expands agency. Fluency frees attention. A teacher's well-designed sequence can give a novice access to questions they could not yet formulate. The relevant distinction is not instruction versus freedom. It is whether instruction is experienced as coherent support for growing capability or as control without intelligible purpose. That is why the best independent evidence points to combinations: autonomy support with structure, challenge with guidance, relevance with disciplinary substance. [10] [11] [24]

The book places the modes on two conceptual dimensions: meaningful engagement and agency. The exact empirical scoring is more complicated than a classroom sketch, but the two-axis map explains the intended logic. Mode What adults may see What may be happening Useful function Main risk Passenger Quiet compliance, minimum effort, invisibility Low investment and little perceived authorship Conserving energy during overload or an unimportant task Drift, skill loss, absence of feedback, shrinking expectations Achiever High grades, preparation, dependability Strong behavioral engagement organized around external evaluation Meeting a deadline, mastering conventions, sustaining routine Risk avoidance, contingent self-worth, exhaustion, strategic rather than deep learning Resister Argument, refusal, avoidance, disruption Agency directed against the learning situation Protecting dignity, exposing injustice, rejecting meaningless work Conflict, exclusion, missed learning, identity hardening around opposition Explorer Questions, initiative, revision, seeking connection Agency directed into meaningful engagement Deep learning, adaptation, ownership, durable curiosity Can be romanticized or confused with unguided activity Passenger. The Passenger is the book's version of quiet quitting. The child is present but has withdrawn the part of the self that risks, wonders, or cares. This can arise from boredom, repeated failure, low expectations, exhaustion, depression, a task that feels irrelevant, or a perfectly rational decision to allocate scarce attention elsewhere. The same behavior can therefore have different causes. A mode names the surface pattern and its relation to agency; it does not diagnose the mechanism beneath it. Achiever. The Achiever is highly engaged in the behaviors schools reward but may exercise less authorship than the performance suggests. The crucial word is may . Some students pursue excellence with curiosity and flexible self-worth. Others become dependent on grades, avoid unfamiliar challenges, and experience mistakes as evidence about personal value. Research on perfectionism supports this distinction: perfectionistic concerns are consistently associated with anxiety and depression, while ambitious striving is more mixed and can coexist with achievement. [17] [18] Resister. The Resister has not lost agency. Agency has become oppositional. This is an important corrective to deficit language. Refusal can be information: the task is too difficult, the relationship is unsafe, the rule is incoherent, the student expects humiliation, or the institution is asking for compliance with something genuinely unjust. But honoring the information does not require romanticizing every refusal. Resistance can protect dignity and still narrow a young person's future. Explorer. The Explorer asks, connects, experiments, seeks feedback, and adapts. The student is neither left alone nor merely obedient. The mode resembles agentic engagement, autonomous motivation, mastery orientation, and self-regulated learning, but it is not identical to any one of them. The Explorer is the book's normative center because agency and engagement point in the same direction. The authors repeatedly state that every mode can be useful. That claim makes the model more realistic. An Explorer may become an Achiever to prepare methodically for an examination. A Passenger may conserve strength during family crisis. A Resister may be the first to reject a harmful norm. The aim is flexible movement, not permanent residence in the favored quadrant. [3]

The book's quantitative backbone comes from a Brookings report produced with Transcend. The report draws on a survey of more than 65,000 US students in grades 3 through 12 and a separate survey of almost 2,000 parents. Using researcher-defined thresholds on school-experience items, the report classified roughly 44 percent of responses as Passenger-supporting, 38 percent as Achiever-supporting, 12 percent as Resister-supporting, and 7 percent as Explorer-supporting, with the displayed percentages affected by rounding. [4] The report's most memorable comparisons concern tenth grade. Twenty-six percent of students said they love school, while 65 percent of parents thought students did. Forty-four percent of students reported learning a lot, compared with 72 percent of parents' perceptions. Twenty-nine percent said school helped them learn about their interests, compared with 71 percent among parents. Thirty-three percent said they developed their own ideas, compared with 69 percent among parents. The direction is striking: adults see a more intellectually alive school experience than students report. [4] But the grammar matters. These are not necessarily answers from each teenager paired with the answer of that teenager's parent. The report describes student and parent surveys as separate. The result supports a population-level perception gap. It does not, without linked dyads, show that 39 percentage points of individual parents are wrong about their own children. Nor do the data explain the gap. Parents may infer from grades and attendance. Students and adults may interpret words such as â€œa lotâ€ or â€œown ideasâ€ differently. Sampling and survey context may matter. The numbers reveal a question worthy of action, not a complete causal story. A second benchmark comes from the US Census Bureau's narrower measure of high school engagement. Its composite asks whether children care about doing well and do required homework while rejecting statements about working only when forced or doing just enough. The 2018 report found roughly one in three children highly engaged. A 2026 update, using 2023 data, estimated 28.5 percent, down from 35.3 percent in 2014. [6] [7] That trend strengthens the concern but also complicates any claim that the number has been stubbornly constant. The Census composite is not the book's four-mode instrument, so its percentages cannot be substituted for Explorer prevalence.

The book did not invent multidimensional engagement. In a foundational 2004 review, Jennifer Fredricks, Phyllis Blumenfeld, and Alison Paris organized a fragmented literature around behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. They also warned that definitions and measures overlapped and that the field often used the same word for different processes. [8] That warning should travel with every use of the four modes. Engagement is an umbrella construct, not a substance that can be read directly from a face. Johnmarshall Reeve and Ching-Mei Tseng later proposed agentic engagement as a fourth aspect: students proactively contribute to the flow of instruction by expressing needs, preferences, questions, and suggestions. In a study of 365 Taiwanese high school students, agentic engagement was distinguishable from behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions and accounted for additional variance in achievement. [9] This is strong conceptual support for the book's agency axis, though a single correlational study in one setting cannot validate the book's entire typology. Self-determination theory supplies the deeper motivational architecture. Across education studies, students tend to function better when they experience autonomy, competence, and relatedness. A meta-analysis of 344 samples involving 223,209 students found that intrinsic motivation was associated with success and well-being, while identified regulation, doing work because it has personal value, was especially relevant to persistence. Externally controlled motives can also sustain performance, but often with less favorable well-being patterns; amotivation is associated with poor outcomes. [13] This evidence refines the book. An Explorer need not love every activity. A teenager may revise algebra because it serves a personally endorsed goal, not because revision itself is delightful. The movement that matters is from â€œI am being made to do thisâ€ toward â€œI understand why this deserves some of my effort,â€ while preserving the right to question the purpose. A second meta-analysis found that support for autonomy from parents, teachers, and peers was related to need satisfaction and more self-determined motivation. Teacher autonomy support showed particularly important associations, and competence was a powerful pathway. [12] This supports the book's practical direction but cautions against making parents the primary engine of a school problem. Family conversations matter. So do classroom design, instruction, peer culture, assessment, resources, disability support, and institutional trust.

The easiest misreading of the book is that agency means leaving teenagers alone. It does not. Autonomy is not the absence of teaching, limits, or expertise. It is the experience that one's actions have intelligible reasons and some degree of willing endorsement. A teacher can be explicit and autonomy supportive. A superficially open task can feel controlling when expectations are hidden. In a study of 133 middle and high school classes, Hyungshim Jang, Johnmarshall Reeve, and Edward Deci found that autonomy support and classroom structure both predicted students' behavioral engagement. The title captured the result: it was not autonomy support or structure, but both. [10] Reeve and Cheon's later review similarly concludes that autonomy-supportive teaching can be learned and can benefit motivation and engagement. Its practices include taking the student's perspective, offering meaningful rationales, using informational rather than pressuring language, acknowledging negative feeling, and creating opportunities for initiative. [11] A 2025 meta-analysis of 94 studies found that autonomy support and structure were positively related rather than opposing forces, and both were positively associated with student engagement. [16] The synthesis matters because educational debate repeatedly stages a false choice between adult guidance and student agency. Novices need models, sequencing, worked examples, feedback, and practice. They also need the work to become increasingly theirs. Mental image: a climbing wall Agency is choosing and solving a route. Structure is the wall, the holds, the rope, the belayer, and the calibrated difficulty. Remove the route choice and the climber merely follows. Remove the structure and there is no climb, only a fall. The same correction applies to productive struggle. Research on â€œproductive failureâ€ does not show that minimally guided discovery is universally superior. It examines carefully designed problem solving before instruction, followed by explicit consolidation. A meta-analysis found advantages under particular conditions, not a license to withhold teaching. [24] Explorer moments should place intellectual responsibility with students while ensuring that the disciplinary ideas become available to them.

The Achiever is the book's sharpest provocation because schools and families usually reward the pattern. The category asks whether performance has become a substitute for purpose. Does the student choose safe tasks, hide confusion, treat feedback as judgment, or experience a grade as a measure of personal worth? If so, excellent results may coexist with a brittle learning strategy. The broader literature makes a distinction the label can blur. A meta-analysis covering 121 studies of children and adolescents found moderate associations between perfectionistic concerns and anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and depression. Perfectionistic strivings had much smaller or more variable associations. [17] Another meta-analytic literature distinguishes mastery goals from performance-avoidance goals: seeking competence and understanding is generally associated with better emotional patterns than trying not to appear incompetent. [18] So high standards are not the pathology. The risk lies in evaluative threat, rigid self-worth, avoidance of error, and control. An ambitious teenager who values the work, seeks difficult feedback, and can recover from a disappointing result may be exploring and achieving at once. The book's quadrant is a prompt to investigate that difference, not evidence that strong students as a group have poor mental health. This is also where adult behavior can become paradoxical. A parent asks about the grade to show interest. The teenager hears that the grade is the interesting part. The parent rescues a difficult assignment to reduce distress. The student learns that struggle signals incapacity. The parent praises effortless brilliance. The child avoids situations in which brilliance might not appear. None of these outcomes is inevitable, but the interaction can turn achievement into surveillance.

The book connects disengagement with absenteeism, lower achievement, risky behavior, and mental health problems. The associations are real. Longitudinal studies find that trajectories of school engagement are related to grades, depression, delinquency, and substance use across adolescence. [19] Engagement also tends to decline, on average, as students move through adolescence, according to a 2026 meta-analysis of longitudinal evidence. [21] Direction is harder. Distress can make concentration, attendance, trust, and initiation difficult. A hostile or pointless school experience can worsen distress. A third factor, such as bullying, learning difficulty, family hardship, sleep loss, discrimination, or chronic illness, can affect both. Cross-sectional mode profiles cannot separate these paths. A recent four-wave study of 431 adolescents is instructive. School engagement and mental health were associated at the level of differences between students, but within-person cross-lagged effects were weaker and inconsistent. One effect suggested mental health predicting later engagement around a school transition. [20] This does not show that engagement never affects well-being. It shows why the phrase â€œdisengagement causes the mental health crisisâ€ outruns current evidence. Causal caution changes practice. If a teenager becomes a Passenger because of untreated depression, a more relevant project may help but is not an adequate mental health response. If resistance follows humiliating classroom treatment, training the student to regulate emotion without changing the environment misses the cause. If academic skills are weak, more choice without instruction may increase helplessness. The mode is the beginning of assessment.

The book favors a developmental and institutional explanation: adolescents seek growing autonomy and relevance, while secondary schooling often becomes more impersonal, evaluative, and controlled. That account is plausible and research aligned. It is not the only account. At least five explanations can produce the same visible withdrawal, and they make different predictions.

avsnitt.rubrik: 1. A mismatch between adolescence and school design
avsnitt.text: As young people become more capable of perspective taking, identity exploration, and independent action, school may offer less choice, weaker relationships, and more performance pressure. Engagement should then improve when students gain meaningful voice, relevance, belonging, and opportunities to affect the learning. Autonomy-supportive teaching and utility-value interventions offer partial support. In one line of experiments, helping students connect coursework to their own lives increased interest and performance particularly for some students with low expectations. [23] The explanation fits the book well, but effects depend on design and context.

A student may withdraw because the work is incomprehensible, too easy, badly sequenced, or built on missing knowledge. The prediction is that diagnostic teaching, explicit explanation, practice, and appropriately calibrated challenge will restore engagement even if choice changes little. Self-determination research places competence alongside autonomy, and the structure evidence supports this account. [10] [12] Dyslexia, ADHD, language barriers, or uneven prior teaching can all be misread as attitude. The four modes allow these causes but do not identify them.

Depression, anxiety, bullying, racism, loneliness, identity threat, family conflict, and sleep loss can turn school into an arena of threat or impossible effort. The prediction is that safety, treatment, accommodation, and trustworthy relationships must change before motivational techniques can do much. The bidirectional evidence between mental health and engagement supports keeping this explanation open. [20] A teenager resisting one classroom but exploring elsewhere may be responding to a relationship, not to learning itself.

avsnitt.rubrik: 4. An attention economy outside the classroom
avsnitt.text: Phones and platforms offer rapid social feedback, novelty, status, and escape. They can fragment attention and make slower rewards less competitive. The book treats technology as an amplifier rather than the root cause, a sensible position. If technology were sufficient, removing devices should reliably create Explorer engagement. It plainly does not. A phone-free room can still be alienating; an online community can support intense learning. Attention ecology matters, but it interacts with purpose, habit, sleep, social need, and instructional quality.

Some disengagement may be real but some is produced by what adults decide to count. A student can be cognitively active while visually still, socially anxious while deeply interested, or strategically compliant in a compulsory system while pursuing demanding learning elsewhere. Cultural norms shape whether questioning appears agentic or disrespectful. Survey thresholds turn continuous answers into categories. The prediction is that modes will shift when measures, settings, or informants change, and that observations, interviews, experience sampling, and work products will not always agree. Explanation What should change the pattern? What it warns adults not to do School-design mismatch Increase meaningful voice, relevance, relationships, and agency Demand compliance more efficiently Competence mismatch Diagnose knowledge, teach explicitly, calibrate challenge Offer choice instead of access to the content Distress or social threat Improve safety, health support, belonging, and accommodations Moralize symptoms as laziness Attention ecology Change device routines, sleep, cue exposure, and task design Assume confiscation supplies meaning Measurement problem Use several informants, settings, times, and forms of evidence Treat one label as the child's essence These explanations are not mutually exclusive. A poorly designed lesson can expose a competence gap, which increases anxiety, which makes the phone more attractive, which produces behavior scored as Passenger. The practical value of the four modes is greatest when they open this causal inquiry. It disappears when the label is offered as the answer.

The book's parental stance can be summarized as coaching without appropriation. Parents should remain interested in learning while giving back ownership of the learner's problems. This is easier to say than to do, especially when schools route every missing task and grade directly to adults. Research on parental involvement supports a careful version of the advice. A meta-analysis of 50 studies in middle school found a positive overall relationship between parental involvement and achievement, with â€œacademic socialization,â€ communicating expectations, linking school to future goals, and discussing strategies, showing the strongest association. Direct homework help did not show the same consistent benefit. [14] A meta-analysis of parent autonomy support found positive associations with achievement and psychosocial functioning, though much of the evidence was correlational. [15] The practical implication is not parental withdrawal. It is a change of level. Instead of taking over the mathematics, help the teenager decide what to ask the teacher. Instead of checking every task, agree on a limited review point. Instead of beginning with â€œWhat did you get?â€, ask what was surprising, confusing, unfair, or worth remembering. Instead of removing every obstacle, distinguish harmful overload from the frustration through which competence grows. Passenger question â€œWhen did this stop feeling worth your attention?â€ Achiever question â€œWhat would you try if the grade could not go down?â€ Resister question â€œWhat are you protecting, and what would a fair next step be?â€ Explorer question â€œWhat do you want to test next, and what support would make it possible?â€ Questions can still become control in interrogative form. Timing matters. So does the adult's ability to tolerate an answer. If a teenager says a course feels pointless, an immediate lecture about future employability teaches that honesty is merely the opening through which persuasion enters. Curiosity requires the possibility that the adult's theory may change. At the same time, agency should not make the child solely responsible for a system adults constructed. A sixteen-year-old can learn to communicate with a teacher, plan work, and recognize a mode. Adults still hold institutional power and must use it when disability support fails, bullying persists, workload is incoherent, or health is at risk. A useful home experiment lasts two weeks, not forever. Choose one recurring conflict. Agree on what belongs to the teenager, what support can be requested, and one time to review the arrangement. Track sleep, distress, completion, and the quality of conversation. If the experiment fails, revise the explanation before increasing control.

For schools, the model exposes a dangerous success criterion. A quiet corridor, submitted work, and respectable examination results may coexist with low authorship. The answer is not to abolish routines or assessment. It is to design for increasing intellectual responsibility. Make purpose inspectable. â€œYou will need this laterâ€ is weak when later is undefined. Explain what problem a method solves, where it fails, and how experts use it. Let students test the rationale against cases. A self-transcendent purpose for learning, connecting schoolwork to contribution beyond the self, has improved self-regulation and persistence in several experiments, though effects are not universal or magical. [22] Offer consequential choices. Choice between blue and green paper is not agency. Students can sometimes choose examples, questions, collaborators, media, pacing within boundaries, or how to demonstrate transfer. The choice must alter the intellectual path while protecting the learning aim. Teach the hidden operations. Planning, asking for clarification, revising, interpreting feedback, and breaking down a task are often demanded without being taught. Agency without these capabilities becomes another advantage for students who acquired them elsewhere. Separate rehearsal from judgment. If every attempt is graded, rational students avoid intellectual risk. Build spaces where errors produce information rather than permanent cost. Preserve clear standards while allowing feedback to change the work. Audit the system from the least powerful seat. A teacher may experience a course as rich in discussion while students experience questions with predetermined answers. Compare adult intent with student report, examples of work, observation, and who actually influences the lesson. The Brookings perception gap makes this audit urgent even if its exact magnitude is not a dyadic measure. [4] Do not make Explorer another compliance demand. Curiosity performed for a rubric is still performance. Some students need quiet participation, preparation before discussion, or culturally different ways of showing initiative. The institution must be willing to be changed by student agency, not merely display it.

avsnitt.rubrik: The Explorer problem in the age of AI
avsnitt.text: In a July 2026 Talks at Google conversation, Winthrop extends the framework into generative AI. The recording is not additional validation of the modes; it is the author's evolving argument, delivered after the book. Her central question is whether AI expands a learner's agency or makes disengagement frictionless. [27] For a Passenger, a general-purpose chatbot can remove the last necessity to think through a task. The student can submit competent prose without constructing the argument, receive an answer without forming the question, and move through a course with less cognitive presence than conventional copying required. For an Achiever, AI can optimize the performance loop: polish every sentence, anticipate a rubric, and reduce the risk of visible imperfection. For a Resister, it can become an efficient way to defeat a demand judged pointless. For an Explorer, the same system can widen the searchable world, generate counterexamples, simulate a difficult audience, or help pursue a question far beyond the available course. [27] The modes therefore describe how a tool is used better than the tool's feature list does. â€œAI in schoolâ€ is not one intervention. The educational effect depends on the learner's purpose, prior knowledge, task design, verification habits, and whether the tool substitutes for or extends a cognitive operation. Winthrop argues for AI-aware pedagogy, not merely AI-powered assignments, alongside protected time for embodied conversation, collaboration, and attention to other people. [27] Her deeper claim is institutional. Schools cannot decide what to automate until they decide what education is for. If the purpose is chiefly production and sorting, faster output looks like success. If the purpose includes judgment, shared inquiry, civic life, and the capacity to learn, some inefficiency is not waste. It is where the capability is formed. The framework's â€œage of agencyâ€ becomes more consequential when a machine can perform the visible product: authorship can no longer be inferred from the artifact. Mental image: the same prompt, four uses The Passenger pastes it. The Achiever perfects it. The Resister uses it to escape the task. The Explorer argues with it, checks it, and leaves with a better question. The difference is not inside the model. It is in the relationship between learner, purpose, and tool. This extension is compelling but still needs outcome research. The talk makes several broad claims about retention, relationships, and students' current AI use that its format cannot fully document. It should generate hypotheses and design principles, not be mistaken for a controlled comparison of the four modes under AI conditions.

The book's survey evidence is primarily American, with the authors' broader qualitative work including the United Kingdom. Its percentages should not be imported into Sweden. Yet Swedish data show a recognizable pattern. In Skolverket's 2024 national survey, about three quarters of students said they liked school and most thought doing well was important. At the same time, only 15 percent of students in grades 7 to 9 said schoolwork was always or often fun, while almost half said it was rarely or never fun. About half of lower and upper secondary students reported school-related stress daily or several times a week, with higher rates among girls. [25] Skolverket's second report found that lower-secondary students were least satisfied with influence and participation, and adults tended to view students' opportunities more positively than students did. In grade 8, perceived influence over how to work and the sense that adults listened were particularly weak. [26] These are not the same questions or scoring rules as the Brookings modes. They cannot establish a Swedish percentage of Passengers or Explorers. They do show the same tension: students can value school and achievement while experiencing little pleasure, control, or relief from stress. The Swedish context also sharpens an equity question. Agency is not merely a personality skill. It depends on whether a system responds. Inviting students to speak without changing anything can teach helplessness more efficiently than never asking. Conversely, structure, special support, predictable routines, and knowledgeable teaching can expand agency for students who find open environments difficult.

The modes have face validity, not diagnostic validity. They describe recognizable patterns and align with established constructs. That is not evidence that statistical analyses consistently recover exactly four groups, that the survey thresholds are optimal, or that mode membership is stable and predictive across cultures and subjects. The materials reviewed for this article did not identify independent peer-reviewed validation of the named four-mode instrument. The axes compress different dimensions. Behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and agentic engagement do not always rise together. A student may think deeply but say little, participate warmly but use shallow strategies, or challenge a teacher without sustaining attention to the subject. One high-low location loses some of that structure. The categories are normatively loaded. Explorer is the desired destination, while the other names carry deficit or danger. That makes the framework easy to remember but can bias observation. Adults may interpret behavior generously when they expect an Explorer and punitively when they expect a Resister. Population association is not individual prognosis. Even if a mode is associated with grades or well-being, it cannot determine what will happen to one student. Nor can the association establish that changing the label changes the outcome. The model can individualize institutional failure. Teaching a teenager to â€œnavigate modesâ€ is useful only if schools also examine schedule, curriculum, assessment, relationships, discrimination, support, and power. A student cannot self-regulate their way out of every bad environment. These limits do not make the model useless. Maps omit. A useful map makes the omission visible and gets revised when the terrain disagrees. The danger begins when an evocative quadrant gains the authority of a test it has not yet become.

avsnitt.rubrik: What we know, infer, and do not know
avsnitt.text: Epistemic status Claim Why Well supported Engagement is multidimensional; agency is a meaningful aspect of learning. Foundational reviews and empirical studies distinguish behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and agentic processes. [8] [9] Well supported Autonomy support works best with competence support and structure. Classroom studies, reviews, and meta-analysis point to complementary effects. [10] [11] [16] Well supported Externally controlled performance and perfectionistic concern can carry well-being costs. Large motivation and perfectionism syntheses distinguish autonomous value and mastery from pressure and evaluative concern. [13] [17] Reasonable inference The four modes can improve conversations by making hidden relations to school discussable. The framework integrates supported constructs, but its conversational benefit needs direct evaluation. Reasonable inference Parents often infer engagement from the school signals they can see. The separate surveys show a perception gap, but not the mechanism or accuracy of individual parent judgments. [4] Not established There are exactly four empirically distinct kinds of student engagement. No independent validation located establishes four natural categories or universal cut points. Not established Disengagement is a single major cause of adolescent mental ill-health. Associations exist, but direction is bidirectional, confounded, and inconsistent at the within-person level. [20] Not established Moving a student into Explorer mode causes all of the favorable outcomes associated with Explorers. The profiling is not a randomized intervention and may reflect prior competence, context, resources, or well-being.

The Disengaged Teen is best read as a change in adult vision. It makes a simple but consequential argument: the student who causes no trouble and produces acceptable results may still be absent from the learning, while the student who resists may still possess the agency education needs. That is not merely a parenting insight. It is a challenge to what institutions count. The book is scientifically strongest when it synthesizes multidimensional engagement, self-determination, agentic engagement, belonging, relevance, and metacognition into a humane language. Its advice to nudge rather than nag, ask before solving, connect work to personally meaningful purposes, and protect productive struggle is broadly congruent with evidence. Its insistence that modes are temporary and context dependent protects the model from becoming crude personality typing. It is weakest when the rhetoric of crisis makes correlation sound causal, when a large cross-sectional survey gives a heuristic typology the appearance of psychometric finality, and when parents seem able to repair problems substantially produced by school design or mental health. The proper response is not to reject the framework. It is to use it at the level the evidence can support. Ask which mode appears here. Ask what function it serves. Then ask what else could produce the same pattern. Change one condition. Watch what happens. Keep the label provisional. A teenager's agency is not demonstrated by choosing the adult's preferred quadrant. It begins when the young person can help revise the map.

artiklar.titel: The mountains are older than their shape
artiklar.amne: Geology Ecology Glaciers Climate Archaeology Hiking Norway Jotunheimen

avsnitt.text: Before looking at a map, decide which Jotunheimen you mean. The mountain region has no single sharp boundary. Store norske leksikon describes it as an area of roughly 3,500 square kilometres between Gudbrandsdalen, Valdres, Sognefjellet, and the districts toward Sogn. Jotunheimen National Park is the protected core, established in 1980 and covering 1,151 square kilometres. The adjoining Utladalen protected landscape adds another 314 square kilometres. [1] [2] This distinction matters. A road, lodge, summit, or trail can belong to the wider Jotunheimen experience without lying inside the national park. It also prevents a familiar mistake: treating a legal boundary as if it created the landscape. The protected area is a modern administrative decision laid over a geological region, an ecological gradient, and a much older human terrain. The region About 3,500 kmÂ², with boundaries that depend partly on geographical convention. The national park 1,151 kmÂ² of the central mountains, protected since 1980. The high point GaldhÃ¸piggen, 2,469 metres above sea level. The route network About 300 kilometres of marked paths within the national park. Twenty six of Norway's twenty seven highest summits lie in Jotunheimen, according to the national encyclopaedia. GaldhÃ¸piggen reaches 2,469 metres. Glittertinden's rock summit reaches 2,452 metres, while Store SkagastÃ¸lstind rises to 2,405 metres. Yet the most useful first fact is not a ranking. It is that great height concentrates changes in weather, snow, vegetation, water, and exposure into short horizontal distances. [1] [11]

A mountain can have several ages. Its minerals may have crystallised at one time, its rocks may have been transported and deformed at another, the land may have been lifted later, and its present ridges and valleys may have been carved later still. Jotunheimen is a particularly good place to keep those clocks apart. Much of the range consists of resistant igneous rocks associated with gabbro, together with granite, syenite, and metamorphosed equivalents. These rocks belong to the Jotun and Valdres nappe complex. Some components formed deep in Precambrian time. A modern synthesis reports orthogneiss in the lower Jotun nappe around 1.65 billion years old, with later metamorphism around 900 million years ago. [3] Those numbers do not mean that a recognisable GaldhÃ¸piggen stood above the landscape a billion years ago. They date parts of the material. The peak is the temporary form that material has now. Mental image: four clocks in one stone Hold a dark block of gabbro in your hand. One clock began when magma cooled. Another records pressure and metamorphism. A third records the collision that moved the rock into a nappe stack. A fourth is still running as frost, streams, gravity, glaciers, and boots alter the exposed surface. Calling the stone â€œoldâ€ is true. Calling the mountain the same age is not.

During the Caledonian mountain building event, roughly four to five hundred million years ago, the ancient continents of Baltica and Laurentia converged. Large sheets of rock were transported over other rocks along major thrust faults. Jotunheimen's resistant rocks became part of that stacked architecture. [3] The original Caledonian range was later worn down. Much later uplift and erosion helped create the high Scandinavian landscape, while repeated Quaternary glaciations excavated the relief seen today. This sequence is why â€œold mountainsâ€ can look sharp. The material is old, but steep arÃªtes and deep troughs are products of renewed erosion, especially by ice.

A glacier does not simply scrape a flat surface. Snow accumulates where topography and wind permit, compacts into ice, and begins to move under gravity. Rock fragments frozen into its base abrade the ground. Meltwater and pressure help loosen blocks. Ice deepens favourable hollows, widens valleys, and carries debris away. Adjacent cirques can retreat toward one another until a narrow ridge remains between them. Jotunheimen therefore contains a vocabulary of glacial form: broad U shaped valleys, steep cirques, narrow arÃªtes, hanging valleys, moraines, polished bedrock, and lakes occupying overdeepened basins. Peaks are left between zones of removal. Their drama is partly negative space. The summits are not monuments added to the landscape. They are remnants between places from which rock was removed. The process is uneven. Rock type, fractures, elevation, snow supply, aspect, and the geometry of former ice flow all matter. A rounded eastern plateau and a knife edged western ridge can belong to the same mountain system without telling the same erosional story. [1]

Jotunheimen stands across a strong climatic gradient. Moist air arriving from the west loses much of its water over the mountains. Western sectors are wetter, more deeply cut, and in places more alpine in profile. The east lies increasingly in a rain shadow, with broader valleys and, in general, a drier climate. [1] [2] This is not a neat dividing line. Weather crosses it, local relief modifies it, and elevation can overwhelm regional averages. But the gradient helps explain why travelling through Jotunheimen feels like moving through more than one range. The western Hurrungane rise in a concentration of sharp summits and deep valleys. Farther east, high roads and plateaux can open a longer horizon, even where nearby slopes remain steep. The gradient also changes life. Snow cover controls the length of the growing season. Moisture affects soils and plant communities. The national park sits at a transition between western and eastern alpine habitats, which contributes to its biological variety. [2]

From Besseggen, two lakes perform a famous comparison. Bessvatnet lies almost 400 metres above Gjende and often appears dark blue. Gjende can appear green, especially later in summer. The contrast is not a filter and not primarily a depth effect. Glacial meltwater carries fine mineral particles, often called rock flour, into Gjende. Suspended particles scatter light and give the water its milky green colour. [2] The colour is erosion made visible. A glacier has ground bedrock into particles small enough to stay suspended. Streams have transported them. The lake has become a temporary display of a mountain being dismantled. Mental image: a mountain held in water Imagine taking a stone and grinding it for centuries until part of it becomes powder. Pour that powder into a lake, keep it suspended with inflowing meltwater, and sunlight will reveal the invisible sediment load. Gjende's green is not separate from the peaks around it. It is the peaks in transit. This also explains why the colour varies. The supply of meltwater and sediment changes through the season and from year to year. Cloud, viewing angle, and surface reflection change what an observer sees. â€œGjende is greenâ€ is a useful description, not a promise of a fixed colour at every hour.

About half of the national park consists of bare rock, loose sediment, ice, or snow. That statistic can make the high country sound biologically empty. It is not. It means that life is distributed in patches, controlled by wind, snow duration, moisture, soil chemistry, and exposure. [2] The official flora account records 36 vascular plant species above 2,000 metres. Glacier buttercup has been found at 2,370 metres below Glittertind, the highest recorded growing vascular plant in Norway. Mountain avens favours calcium rich ground. Dwarf willow compresses the architecture of a tree into a plant that hugs the surface, where wind is weaker and warmth can accumulate. [6] These are not simply miniature lowland plants. Alpine survival involves timing. A plant may wait under snow, grow rapidly after melt, flower during a short window, and endure frost in any month. Snow can be both shelter and constraint. A late melting snowbed is protected from winter wind but has less summer in which to complete growth. Bird life also follows the mosaic. The protected area records more than one hundred bird species, about 75 of them breeding within the national park itself. Wetlands, willow zones, lakes, cliffs, and exposed high ground each offer different food and nesting conditions. [2]

â€œReindeer in Jotunheimenâ€ hides an important distinction. In eastern Jotunheimen, the reindeer are domesticated animals belonging to herding communities. Wild reindeer occur in Hurrungane and the western part of the protected area. A distant animal is therefore not automatically evidence of a wild herd. [7] Wolverines are the large predator whose traces a visitor is most likely to encounter, although seeing the animal itself is uncommon. Small rodents, meanwhile, can fluctuate dramatically between years. Their abundance affects predators and the wider food web. The quietness of one walking day is a poor census of an alpine ecosystem.

The usual tourism story begins with nineteenth century explorers and mountain lodges. Human presence begins much earlier. Archaeological traces near Gjende, Russvatnet, Tyinosen, and Koldedalen reach back toward 3000 BCE. Hunters used pitfalls, stone hides, temporary shelters, and routes through the high ground. Fishing, trapping, grazing, and movement between districts made the mountains a working landscape. [8] This changes how a path can be read. A line through a pass is not only a recreational solution to modern topography. It may be part of a much older logic: where animals move, where snow melts, where a packhorse can pass, where water is available, and where a traveller can find shelter before weather closes in. Pastoral farming later added summer farms, livestock movement, haymaking, and grazing. These practices altered vegetation and left buildings, fences, tracks, and place names. â€œUntouched wildernessâ€ is therefore too simple. Jotunheimen contains large areas with little permanent settlement, but absence of houses is not absence of history.

avsnitt.rubrik: When the ice became an archive
avsnitt.text: Climate warming has exposed artefacts from ice patches in and around Jotunheimen. Ice archaeology is not the same as ordinary excavation. Organic objects can remain frozen for centuries, then decay rapidly once exposed. Archaeologists must search newly melted surfaces, record precise context, and conserve finds before weather, animals, or another freeze moves or destroys them. A large study of reindeer hunting at Norwegian ice patches assembled more than 2,000 finds and 153 radiocarbon dates. The chronology extends from around 4000 BCE to recent times and reveals changing intensity in high altitude hunting. The record is not a simple curve of population. Preservation, snow conditions, reindeer behaviour, trade, technology, and human activity all influence what survives and what is found. [9] At Lendbreen, an ice patch and mountain pass east of the main national park, finds included clothing, everyday objects, transport equipment, cairns, a shelter, and the remains of pack animals. The evidence indicates use from around AD 300 through the end of the Middle Ages, with especially intense traffic during the Viking Age and medieval period. [10] Mental image: a road that disappears into ice Picture a traveller following cairns toward a pass. A mitten is lost. A horse drops a shoe. Snow covers both. The route falls out of use, the objects enter ice, and centuries later warming returns them to the surface. The find is not treasure dropped in an empty wilderness. It is evidence that the ice itself once lay across a road. The archive has a cruel condition: the same melting that makes an artefact visible also starts its destruction. Discovery and loss are coupled.

The mountains existed before their modern regional name. Geologist Baltazar Mathias Keilhau used â€œJotunfjeldeneâ€ in 1823. Poet Aasmund Olavsson Vinje used â€œJÃ¸tunheimenâ€ and â€œJÃ¸tunfjelliâ€ in 1862. The name draws on JÃ¶tunheimr, the realm of the jÃ¶tnar in Norse mythology. It helped turn a collection of local mountains and routes into a national imaginative landscape. [1] That naming came during a period of exploration, mapping, national romanticism, and organised tourism. The botanist Christen Smith climbed GaldhÃ¸piggen in 1813. Keilhau and Christian Boeck travelled through the range in 1820. The Norwegian Trekking Association, founded in 1868, opened Gjendebu in 1871. It is the oldest DNT cabin still operating. [1] [12] Modern hiking inherited both older routes and newer ways of seeing. Cairns and red T marks make movement legible. Guidebooks organise summits into objectives. Cabins turn a continuous landscape into daily stages. None of this makes the experience artificial. It means that a hiking landscape is partly an infrastructure of attention.

Jotunheimen's glaciers are remnants of colder conditions, but they are not static relics. A reconstruction of the Little Ice Age maximum identified 233 glaciers covering about 290 square kilometres. By 2003, their combined area had declined by about 35 percent and their average flow length by about 34 percent. These percentages compare 2003 with each glacier's reconstructed Little Ice Age maximum, not with a single modern baseline year. [4] Year to year weather still matters. Norway's Water Resources and Energy Directorate reported that all nine reference glaciers measured in 2024 had negative annual mass balance, even though their summer balance was less negative than the 1991 to 2020 average. Of 35 glacier outlets measured that year, 34 retreated. Jotunheimen reference glaciers in the programme include Storbreen, Hellstugubreen, and GrÃ¥subreen. [5] A single snowy winter or cool summer can slow loss or produce a temporary local gain. It does not cancel the longer retreat. Conversely, a dramatic photograph of one glacier cannot quantify the entire region. Long measurements, mapped outlines, and mass balance records are needed because a glacier responds to both accumulation and melt. Retreat changes more than scenery. It alters meltwater timing, exposes unstable sediment and rock, changes access routes, reveals archaeological material, and removes ice that stores a record of past conditions. The safest practical conclusion is also the most scientifically honest: glacier terrain must be assessed as it is now, not as remembered from an old map or photograph.

avsnitt.rubrik: Choose a question, then a route
avsnitt.text: Route choice becomes clearer when it starts with the experience sought. Do you want the visual contrast between Gjende and Bessvatnet, Norway's highest summit, an eastern viewpoint, or a short walk with time left to study weather and light? Distance alone cannot answer this. Exposure, ascent, surface, navigation, transport, and the possibility of retreat matter. Route Published outline What defines it Decision that matters Besseggen About 14 km, often around 8 hours A long ridge traverse above Gjende, with steep and exposed sections Direction, wind, boat logistics, and confidence on the ridge Most walkers take the boat to Memurubu and return to Gjendesheim on foot. GaldhÃ¸piggen from Spiterstulen About 9 hours return A long summit day that avoids glacier travel when the same route is used both ways Energy, weather, snow, and the discipline to return by the non-glacier route GaldhÃ¸piggen from Juvasshytta About 6 to 7 hours return A shorter summit route that crosses Styggebreen A guide and roped glacier party are required for the glacier crossing Bitihorn from BÃ¥tskaret About 3.7 km and 2 hours return Short, steep, partly loose, and exposed Do not translate short distance into low consequence Synshorn About 4.3 km and 2 hours return A moderate eastern viewpoint above Bygdin Useful when the aim is a viewpoint rather than a major summit day KnutshÃ¸e About 12.7 km and 5 hours Exposed scrambling and a demanding ridge circuit It is sometimes marketed as Besseggen's smaller sibling, not as its easy substitute The figures above are route descriptions, not guarantees. UT classifies both terrain and effort, and conditions can move a route beyond a person's normal margin. Besseggen is commonly walked from Memurubu toward Gjendesheim because the steepest scrambling is then uphill. The opposite direction changes both the physical task and the psychological exposure. [13] GaldhÃ¸piggen illustrates why a summit name is not a route description. From Spiterstulen, a same-way return avoids glacier crossing, although it remains a long high mountain day. From Juvasshytta, the normal route crosses Styggebreen and requires glacier equipment, rope team competence, and normally a guide. Combining routes without recognising that transition can turn a walking plan into unplanned glacier travel. [14] [15] Bitihorn makes the opposite point. A short outing can contain exposed and loose terrain. Synshorn offers a less committing viewpoint in the same broad eastern gateway. KnutshÃ¸e adds scrambling and exposure. Their kilometres are not a common currency. [16] [17] [18]

avsnitt.rubrik: The mountain is a decision system
avsnitt.text: Norway's Mountain Code is concise because mountain safety is less about memorising hazards than about making repeated decisions. Plan and report the route. Adapt it to ability and conditions. Check weather and avalanche information. Be prepared for cold and bad weather even on a short trip. Carry navigation equipment. Choose safe terrain. Turn back in time. Conserve energy and seek shelter when necessary. [21] In Jotunheimen, weather can change quickly and winter conditions can occur in summer. Fog removes distant landmarks and can make cairns ambiguous. Wind changes balance and perceived exposure. Rain turns rock and roots slippery. Stream levels respond to rain and melt. Snow can hide the path or make a slope harder than its summer grade suggests. [19] A useful plan has at least three layers: Before departure Current forecast, route condition, transport, daylight, map, clothing, water, food, and a realistic turnaround rule. During the walk Compare actual time, weather, surface, group condition, and navigation with the plan. At the margin Turn around while retreat is still easy, not when every warning has become decisive. After a change Tell the relevant person if the route or return time changes. A phone, satellite communicator, or emergency beacon can improve communication. It does not make steep wet rock less slippery, create a safe glacier route, or replace map, compass, judgement, and a turnaround decision. Rescue communication is a layer of resilience, not a permit to spend the rest of the margin. Glaciers require a separate threshold. The national park administration warns that glacier walking without rope, correct equipment, and knowledge is dangerous and recommends joining a local guide. Crevasses can be hidden by snow. A route that merely touches a glacier is therefore a different category from a marked mountain path. [2] Use current services before departure. Varsom publishes avalanche and other natural hazard information. The Norwegian Public Roads Administration provides live road and mountain pass status. UT and the relevant cabin or boat operator provide route and transport details. Valdresflye on county road 51 reaches 1,389 metres and is a seasonal mountain road, so its status belongs in the departure check, not in a timeless itinerary. [22] [23] Protected landscape rules: The right to roam permits low impact travel, but it is not a right to leave no responsibility behind. In the park, drones are prohibited. Do not build new cairns. Observe fire rules, dog leash periods, camping distance from inhabited buildings, and any local restrictions. Carry out all waste. [19]

Cabins are part of Jotunheimen's transport system. A staffed lodge can shorten the distance between shelter and a route. A self service cabin changes what must be carried. A boat across Gjende changes the direction and timing of a traverse. Booking is therefore not separate from route planning. DNT cabins range from staffed lodges to self service and no service cabins. Opening dates, access, food, key requirements, and booking arrangements vary. Check the individual cabin on UT or DNT rather than assuming that one cabin's system applies to the next. [24] One small item deserves explicit mention because it is easy to discover too late: DNT requires a sleeping bag liner or ordinary bed linen when using cabin bedding. A sleeping bag alone is not the same thing, and a duvet should not be used without a liner or linen. [20] The larger principle is simple. Shelter, food, transport, and route are one plan. If a late boat, full cabin, closed road, or missed meal changes the day, the mountain does not pause while logistics are repaired.

avsnitt.rubrik: What is known, inferred, and changing
avsnitt.text: Jotunheimen invites confident stories. A disciplined exploration marks where confidence comes from. Claim type Example How to treat it Measured or mapped National park area, summit elevations, glacier outlines, and annual mass balance Cite the responsible survey or institution, including baseline and year. Well supported interpretation Glacial erosion produced major valleys, cirques, and ridges Explain the mechanism without pretending every landform has one simple cause. Archaeological inference An ice patch pass served traffic and transport Connect objects, dates, route markers, and context, while allowing for preservation bias. Variable observation Gjende looks green or a route takes eight hours Treat colour, timing, water, snow, and visibility as conditional. Live operational fact A road is open, a boat runs, a bridge is installed, or a warning is active Check immediately before departure. Do not fossilise it into an evergreen article. Route duration is especially easy to misuse. A published estimate describes a reference outing under some set of assumptions. It does not measure your group, today's wind, lingering snow, queueing at a scramble, photography stops, or the time needed to make a careful retreat. The same caution applies to glacier percentages. â€œThirty five percent smallerâ€ is meaningful only with its defined comparison, the reconstructed Little Ice Age maximum and the 2003 map. Removing the baseline would make the sentence shorter and the knowledge worse. [4]

A first glance at Jotunheimen separates things: summit from valley, green lake from grey rock, trail from wilderness, human history from natural history. A closer look reconnects them. The resistant rock helps peaks persist. Fractures and structure guide erosion. Ice excavates valleys and grinds sediment. Meltwater carries that sediment into Gjende. Snow duration and ground chemistry organise alpine plants. Reindeer and people find routes through the same topographic constraints. Cairns and cabins turn those routes into a modern recreational network. Warming retreats the ice, changes present travel, and uncovers evidence of older travel. This is the red thread through Jotunheimen: the landscape is not a collection of scenic objects. It is a set of processes moving at different speeds. Rock crystallises, continents collide, glaciers pulse, plants seize a short summer, paths accumulate footsteps, and a walker makes the next decision in minutes. The deepest view from a summit is not that the world has stopped beneath you. It is that everything in the view is moving, only on different clocks. Go to Jotunheimen for the height if height is what first draws you. Then notice what height gathers together: ancient material, young relief, thin soil, rapid weather, compressed ecology, old roads, modern infrastructure, and decisions with consequences. The mountains become larger when they stop being only tall.
